Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of dark water. In its center floated a single seed, silver as moonlit bone. The seed dreamed of warmth, and from that dream came Ember-Wren, a tiny bird with feathers of fire.

Ember-Wren flew across the endless water, but there was nowhere to rest. So she plucked one burning feather from her breast and dropped it into the deep. The water hissed, steamed, and rose into mountains. She dropped another feather, and valleys opened like cupped hands. A third became the sun, which climbed into the sky and laughed light over everything.

Yet the world was silent. Ember-Wren grew lonely, so she sang. Where her song touched stone, trees unfolded. Where it touched mud, animals shook themselves awake. Where it touched shadow, people opened their eyes and asked who had called them.

“I did,” said Ember-Wren, now dim and small.

The people, seeing her fading, built the first hearth and fed it twigs, grass, and gratitude. Ember-Wren settled inside the flame, warm again. That is why every fire dances like wings, and why, when people gather near it, they remember the song that made them.

Before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and above it drifted Aro, the Moth Who Carried Fire. In her wings slept every star, but she was afraid to open them, for the dark was cold and jealous.

One night, a turtle rose from the deep and said, “Little Aro, I am tired of swimming without a shore. Give me one spark, and I will hold it safely.”

Aro trembled, but she shook a single ember from her wing. It fell upon the turtle’s back and spread into warm clay. Mountains grew where his shell was ridged, and valleys formed where it was smooth. Trees pushed up like green thoughts, and rivers slid down to remember the sea.

The dark hissed and reached to swallow the new land. So Aro opened both wings at last. Stars scattered across the sky, burning tiny holes through night’s cloak. The jealous dark fled into caves and deep wells, where it still mutters.

Aro’s wings became the moon, pale from her giving. The turtle sleeps beneath the earth, and when he dreams, the ground shakes. People light fires to thank the moth, and plant seeds to honor the turtle.

Myth: Before dawn learned its name, the world was only black water and a silence without edges. Above it fluttered Aro, the small moth whose wings held hidden sparks. She feared the dark, which whispered, “Keep your light folded, and I will spare you.”

From the deep rose Old Turtle, weary of swimming forever. “Give me one spark,” he said, “and I will make it a place to rest.”

Aro opened one trembling wing. A coal fell onto Turtle’s shell, and it softened into earth. The ridges became mountains, the hollows became lakes, and green forests grew like moss upon his back. But the dark, angered by this warm island, gathered itself into a great mouth.

Aro knew one ember was not enough. She spread both wings wide, scattering stars like seeds. Some became the sun, some became hearth-fire, and one pale spark became the moon, so travelers would not forget courage at night.

The dark fled into caves and deep roots. Old Turtle slept beneath the new land, holding it steady. When he stirs, the hills tremble. And every moth that circles a flame is Aro’s child, searching for the first brave light.

Myth: Before dawn learned its name, the world was only a black sea breathing under a roof of silence. Upon the waves drifted Ember-Wren, a bird no larger than a child’s hand, carrying a coal in her heart. She searched for a branch, a stone, even a thorn, but found nothing that would hold her.

At last she sang to the coal, and it answered by becoming brave. Ember-Wren drew it from her breast and cast it into the water. Steam rose like white giants. Where the coal touched, the sea hardened into the first island, red and warm. She beat her wings, scattering sparks. Each spark became a star; each fallen ash became soil.

Still the island was lonely, so Ember-Wren scratched furrows with her tiny claws. From them grew cedars, reeds, and flowers with faces turned toward her. She sang again, and beasts stepped from the shadows of the trees. The last note she saved for humankind, shaping it gently from breath and clay.

But her heart had grown dim. The people gathered dry branches and made a nest of flame. Ember-Wren entered it gladly. Since then, every hearth shelters her, and every morning is her small red wing opening again.

Myth: Before the sun had a path, the world was a lidless bowl of night-water, and nothing had a name. Over it flew Ember-Wren, small as a thumb, with a red coal hidden beneath her feathers. She looked for a place to land, but the sea only rolled and whispered.

From below rose Grandmother Turtle, her shell dark and empty. “Little flame-bird,” she said, “my back is tired of waves. Give me warmth, and I will carry it.”

Ember-Wren opened her breast and dropped the coal upon the shell. It spread into clay, then hills, then mountains. In the low places, rain gathered and remembered the sea. Ember-Wren shook her wings, and sparks leapt upward to become stars. One great spark became the sun; one quiet spark became the moon.

Yet the new earth was bare. So Ember-Wren sang into the soil. Trees lifted their green hands. Animals came blinking from roots and stones. Last, she shaped people from mud, breath, and a note of longing.

The coal had nearly spent her. The people built the first hearth and invited her inside. Grandmother Turtle slept beneath them all. When the ground trembles, she is dreaming; when fires dance, Ember-Wren is still singing.

Myth: Before morning had a path to follow, the world was a bowl of dark water, deep and unremembering. Above it wandered Aro, the ash-gray moth, carrying a thousand sparks beneath her folded wings. She longed to shine, yet the darkness coiled around her and murmured, “Light is lonely. Stay hidden.”

Then Old Turtle lifted his head from the endless sea. Barnacles crowned him like old stars. “Little flame-bearer,” he said, “I have swum since before time. Give me warmth, and I will give it a back to stand upon.”

Aro shook loose one ember. It landed on Turtle’s shell and spread into red clay. His ridges rose as mountains; his scars filled with rivers; his slow breath pushed forests from the soil. Animals crept from roots and stones, blinking at the newborn air.

The darkness roared and poured itself over the land. Aro, frightened but no longer willing to fold herself away, opened both wings. Sparks flew upward into constellations, downward into hearths, and eastward into the sun. Her palest ember became the moon, keeper of quiet roads.

Old Turtle still bears the earth, dreaming below us. When people share fire, Aro’s courage wakes again, and night loosens its teeth.
